Tutorial: Your First Coverage Study

Source: vignettes/tutorial-first-study.qmd

What you will build

In about fifteen minutes you will run a complete Monte Carlo study: does the Sobel (delta-method) confidence interval for the indirect effect abab cover the true value 95% of the time, and how often does the Sobel test reject when the indirect effect is zero?

You will:

  1. write a data-generating model (DGM) as a medsim_scenario();
  2. write an estimator that returns an estimate, a confidence interval and a p-value;
  3. tell medsim the true value of the estimand;
  4. run the study, first as a 20-replication smoke test, then for real;
  5. read coverage, type I error and power, each with its Monte Carlo standard error (MCSE).

The #> output shown below comes from medsim 0.6.0. Because medsim seeds every replication from the scenario name and the replication number, your run should reproduce these numbers.

Step 1: Describe the data-generating model

A scenario bundles a data generator with the parameters that generated the data. This helper builds a simple X→M→YX \to M \to Y model with paths aa and bb:

library(medsim)

make_scenario <- function(a, b, name) {
  medsim_scenario(
    name = name,
    description = sprintf("a = %.2f, b = %.2f", a, b),
    data_generator = function(n = 200) {
      X <- rnorm(n)
      M <- a * X + rnorm(n)
      Y <- b * M + rnorm(n)
      data.frame(X = X, M = M, Y = Y)
    },
    params = list(a = a, b = b, indirect = a * b)
  )
}

scenarios <- list(
  make_scenario(0.39, 0.39, "Medium"),       # ab = 0.1521
  make_scenario(0,    0.39, "Null (a = 0)")  # ab = 0
)

The generator must take the sample size as its argument n. medsim_run() supplies it from the configuration (medsim_config(n = ), 200 unless you set it), so the default n = 200 in the signature only matters when you call the generator by hand.

Two scenarios are enough to answer both questions. Under “Medium” the rejection rate is power; under “Null (a = 0)” it is the type I error.

Checkpoint

medsim_validate_scenario(scenarios[[1]]) should return TRUE. To eyeball the generator, call head(scenarios[[1]]$data_generator(5)).

Scenario names are seeds

A replication’s random-number seed is derived from the scenario name and the replication number. Renaming a scenario therefore changes its data. Choose names once, before the production run.

Step 2: Write the estimator

A method is any function of (data, params) that returns a named list. The names follow a convention, and the analysis functions find their columns by it:

Name Read by
indirect accuracy metrics (bias, RMSE, …)
indirect_se the model-based SE in medsim_analyze_performance()
indirect_ci_lower, indirect_ci_upper medsim_analyze_coverage()
indirect_p medsim_analyze_power() 
sobel <- function(data, params) {
  fm <- summary(lm(M ~ X, data = data))$coefficients
  fy <- summary(lm(Y ~ X + M, data = data))$coefficients
  a  <- fm["X", "Estimate"]; sa <- fm["X", "Std. Error"]
  b  <- fy["M", "Estimate"]; sb <- fy["M", "Std. Error"]
  se <- sqrt(b^2 * sa^2 + a^2 * sb^2)   # first-order delta method

  list(
    indirect          = a * b,
    indirect_se       = se,
    indirect_ci_lower = a * b - 1.96 * se,
    indirect_ci_upper = a * b + 1.96 * se,
    indirect_p        = 2 * pnorm(-abs(a * b / se))
  )
}

Checkpoint

Call the method once by hand before handing it to the runner: str(sobel(scenarios[[1]]$data_generator(), scenarios[[1]]$params)) should print five numbers.

Step 3: State the truth

Coverage and bias need the true value. compute_truth has the same signature as the method and returns the true value of each quantity you want scored. Here the truth is a parameter of the DGM:

truth <- function(data, params) list(indirect = params$indirect)

For estimands without a closed form, compute_truth can do the expensive work (for example, a large Monte Carlo integration). medsim computes it once per scenario and caches it in the output directory.

Step 4: Smoke test, then the real run

Always run the "test" configuration first: 20 replications, a few seconds, and it catches a broken method before you spend hours on it.

smoke <- medsim_run(sobel, scenarios, medsim_config("test"),
                    compute_truth = truth)
table(failed = !is.na(smoke$results$error))
#> failed
#> FALSE
#>    40

Twenty replications are too few to conclude anything. The smoke run reports 100% coverage in both scenarios, which says more about noise than about Sobel. The real run uses 500 replications per scenario:

config  <- medsim_config("local", n_replications = 500)
results <- medsim_run(sobel, scenarios, config, compute_truth = truth)

Where files go

medsim_run() writes cached truth values to the configuration’s output_dir (simulation_results_local/ here). Pass medsim_config(..., output_dir = tempdir()) to keep a scratch run out of your project.

Step 5: Read the results

Coverage 

cov <- medsim_analyze_coverage(results, ci_levels = 0.95)
cov$by_scenario[, c("scenario", "coverage", "coverage_mcse", "n_valid")]
#>       scenario coverage coverage_mcse n_valid
#> 1       Medium    0.944   0.010282412     500
#> 2 Null (a = 0)    0.960   0.008763561     500

Both rates sit within two MCSEs of .95, so with 500 replications there is no evidence of under- or over-coverage in either scenario.

Type I error and power 

pw <- medsim_analyze_power(results, alpha = 0.05)
pw$by_scenario
#>       scenario parameter power n_valid alpha
#> 1       Medium  indirect 0.996     500  0.05
#> 2 Null (a = 0)  indirect 0.040     500  0.05

medsim_analyze_power() reports the rejection rate, whatever the truth. In the null scenario that rate is the type I error, .040. Its MCSE is .05×.95/500≈.0097\sqrt{.05 \times .95 / 500} \approx .0097, so .040 is within about one MCSE of the nominal .05.

Bias and standard errors 

medsim_analyze_performance(results)
#>       scenario parameter          bias   bias_mcse empirical_se   model_se
#> 1       Medium  indirect  0.0013953010 0.001757397   0.03929660 0.03969967
#> 2 Null (a = 0)  indirect -0.0008496464 0.001257212   0.02811212 0.02846886
#>         rmse n_converged n_failed
#> 1 0.03928207         500        0
#> 2 0.02809685         500        0

The model-based SE (model_se, the average Sobel SE) agrees with the empirical SD of the estimates (empirical_se) to within 1.5%: the delta method is accurate at n=200n = 200 for these paths.

What you learned

  • A study is three functions (a generator, a method and a truth) plus a configuration.
  • Output-name conventions (_ci_lower, _ci_upper, _p, _se) are how the analysis functions find their inputs.
  • Every rate is an estimate. Read it next to its MCSE, and size the run so that the MCSE is small enough to answer your question (see medsim_nsim_for_mcse()).

Exercises

  1. Add a scenario with a=b=0a = b = 0. The Sobel test is known to be very conservative there. How far below .05 does its rejection rate fall?
  2. Rerun with a sample size of 50: medsim_config("local", n_replications = 500, n = 50). Which breaks down first: coverage or the agreement between model_se and empirical_se?
  3. How many replications would you need for a coverage MCSE of .005? Check your answer with medsim_nsim_for_mcse(0.005).
